title: Quality: DoR, DoD, registers, MoSCoW, testing and debt
blurb: Put quality information in the right place, apply the Definitions of Ready and Done, and choose the right agile quality technique for a scenario.
question: Callowmere University's web team has a story that passes its functional tests but still has two accessibility defects. The product owner wants to count it as 'almost done'. What does PRINCE2 Agile say, and where is the rule recorded?

teach.body: The quality practice records what users need from the products and how that will be achieved. In PRINCE2 Agile, quality is driven by the requirements in the project backlog and kept in line with the quality management approach through a cycle of quality planning, quality control and product acceptance. If the business has its own design, development and testing procedures, they may be used instead, with that choice recorded as a tailoring decision in the PID.

teach.body: Test first, or at least test as you go, is the preferred agile pattern, and the decision about how much is possible should be made early. Take care when moving the idea from software, where automated builds can be tested in minutes, to other products such as a training course or a campaign, which cannot be rebuilt that quickly. Validation asks whether you are building the right thing; verification asks whether you are building the thing right.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Callowmere's Student Support Hub
teach.body: The web team's Definition of Done lacks testing with assistive technology, so Rebecca Lyle, the product owner, and the team add screen-reader testing to it. Project manager Jamal Hussain records the agile testing methods of the web team and Northmere in the quality management approach. Each round of testing with the student design panel goes in the quality register with its result. Approval from the data protection officer becomes a Definition of Ready criterion for any story storing health data.

teach.text: Traps: the quality register records quality activities and results, while the product register records products and their status. The DoR applies before work starts and the DoD decides completion. There is no 'almost done'. Agile behaviours and agile testing methods are documented and assured in the quality management approach, not the communication management approach. Refactoring tidies structure; technical debt is the cost of not doing so.

items: Quality is driven by the project backlog: plan, control, accept, every iteration.
An organization's own procedures may be used; record that as tailoring in the PID.
DoR = ready to start; DoD = complete; partly done stories are split, defects mean not done.
Quality register = checks and results; product register = products and status.
Refactoring, technical debt (with tolerance), test first or as you go, A/B testing.

summary: You can now put quality information in the right artifact, from the product backlog and quality management approach to the quality and product registers. You can also apply the Definitions of Ready and Done and choose refactoring, technical debt tolerances, test-first thinking or A/B testing to fit a scenario.

A.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's Smart Maintenance project has completed Release 1. Robert Kale, who provides project assurance, asks where he can see which quality checks were carried out on the sensor installations, when they took place, who did them and whether each one passed. Where should this information be recorded?
A.why: The quality register summarizes all planned and completed quality activities: method, planned and actual dates, responsibilities, pass or fail result and records (Table 9.1).

whyNot.0: The product register lists the products a plan requires and their status, not the details of each quality check.
whyNot.1: The quality management approach describes how quality will be managed; it does not record individual checks.
whyNot.3: The team dashboard shows a team's progress at a glance; the formal record of quality activities is the quality register.

A.q: Callowmere University's web team is in a team planning workshop. A story for booking a counselling appointment has its who, what and why, measurable and prioritized acceptance criteria, and the data protection officer's approval for storing booking data. The team agrees work on it can start. Which agreement sets out the criteria the story has met?
A.why: The Definition of Ready sets the criteria an item must meet before work begins: clear objectives and scope, information, resources and dependencies in place (9.3.2.1).

whyNot.1: The Definition of Done sets the criteria for an item to count as complete, not ready to start.
whyNot.2: The quality register records quality activities and their results, not the criteria for starting work.
whyNot.3: The product register records products and their status, not readiness criteria.

A.q: Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project is in initiation. Coinbridge Payments' team uses automated testing on every build of its payment service. Project manager Rhys Pengelly wants the agile testing methods of Coinbridge and the in-house teams documented and assured. Where should they be recorded?
A.why: The quality management approach sets out quality techniques, standards and responsibilities, and is where agile ways of working and testing methods, including suppliers', are documented and assured (Table 9.1).

whyNot.0: The commercial management approach covers how suppliers are engaged and contracted, not the testing methods they use.
whyNot.2: The communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication, not testing methods.
whyNot.3: The quality register records individual quality activities and results, not the methods to be used.

B.q: Easterholm County Council's Care Online project is nearing the end of Release 1. The board asks for a list of all the products in the Release 1 plan and whether each has been approved and accepted yet. Some products have passed their quality review but have not yet been accepted. Where should the project manager look?
B.why: The product register lists all products a plan requires and their status, including approval and acceptance dates (Table 9.1).

whyNot.0: The quality register shows quality activities and pass or fail results, which do not show whether a product has been accepted.
whyNot.1: The release map shows releases and features at a high level, not each product's approval and acceptance status.
whyNot.2: The issue register records issues, not the status of every product in a plan.

B.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's e-commerce team restructures the code behind the live stock display so that it will be easier to change in Release 2. Customers see no difference in how the display looks or behaves. Which quality technique is the team applying?
B.why: Refactoring changes the internal structure of a product without changing its external behaviour (9.4.1).

whyNot.0: A/B testing compares two versions with users; here there is one version and no user comparison.
whyNot.2: Test-first development writes tests before the work; the scenario describes restructuring existing code.
whyNot.3: Validation checks that the right thing is being built; the team is improving structure, not checking needs.

B.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's digital team shows half of the tenants on the pilot estate one version of the online repair form and half another version. It then compares how many tenants in each group complete a report. Which quality technique is being used?
B.why: A/B testing compares two versions of a product or feature with users to see which is more effective (9.4.3).

whyNot.0: Verification checks that the product is built correctly to its specification, not which of two versions users prefer.
whyNot.1: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour; two different versions are being compared here.
whyNot.3: Behaviour-driven development extends test-first development using language users understand; it is not a comparison of versions.

C.q: Callowmere University's web team has finished a story for the self-referral form. It passes its functional tests but still has two known accessibility defects. Product owner Rebecca Lyle proposes marking it 'almost done' and counting its points in this sprint. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the remaining defects are small and known
Yes, because partly done stories are split and moved
No, because work is either done or not done
No, because the Definition of Ready was not met
C.why: Under the Definition of Done an item is either done or not done; there is no 'almost done', and work with defects is not done (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Known defects still mean the story fails the DoD, so it cannot be counted as complete.
whyNot.1: Splitting moves a genuinely done part to done and returns the rest to the backlog; counting the whole story as 'almost done' is not splitting, and work with defects is not done.
whyNot.3: The DoR applies before work starts; the problem here is completion, which the DoD governs.

C.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's aerospace quality system has its own procedures for designing, testing and approving any change to how machines are maintained. In initiation, project manager Andrea Lucas uses these procedures instead of the standard PRINCE2 Agile quality procedure and records this as a tailoring decision in the PID. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the business may use its own procedure
Yes, because the quality manager approves all changes
No, because the PRINCE2 Agile procedure is mandatory
No, because tailoring belongs in the quality register
C.why: An alternative procedure may be used when the business has its own design, development and testing procedures, and that choice is documented as a tailoring decision in the PID (9.3.1).

whyNot.1: Who approves changes does not explain the verdict: the reason the business's own procedure may replace the standard one is the tailoring allowed in 9.3.1.
whyNot.2: PRINCE2 Agile permits an organization's own procedures, recorded as tailoring in the PID.
whyNot.3: The quality register records quality activities and results; tailoring decisions are recorded in the PID.

C.q: Larkspur Rail's app carries a large amount of technical debt from a rushed redesign. In initiation, the board sets a tolerance for the level of technical debt and asks the project manager to raise an exception if the debt is forecast to become too significant. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
options: Yes, because technical debt is repaid by external redesign
Yes, because tolerances can be applied to technical debt
No, because technical debt is managed through the team DoD
No, because exceptions in agile relate to time and cost
C.why: Tolerances may be applied to technical debt, and if the debt is forecast to become too significant it causes an exception (9.4.2).

whyNot.0: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing external behaviour; 'external redesign' is not how debt is described or repaid.
whyNot.2: The DoD helps stop new debt being accepted as done, but it does not replace a tolerance for the debt that already exists.
whyNot.3: Time and cost have zero tolerance by default; exceptions in agile are often about what is delivered, including quality.

reteach.title: Running a bakery's order book
reteach.question: A small bakery takes custom cake orders. When is an order ready to start, when is a cake done, and where does the baker look to answer each kind of question?

blocks.h: Ready, done and the two lists
blocks.body: An order is ready to start when the flavour, size, date and allergy details are confirmed and the ingredients are in: that is the Definition of Ready. A cake is done when it is baked, iced, checked against the order and boxed. Half-iced is not done. The baker keeps one list of every cake ordered and its status (product register) and a log of every taste test and allergy check with its result (quality register).

head: Bakery
PRINCE2 Agile
rows: List of cakes and their status
Log of taste tests and results

blocks.text: A cake with a cracked top is not 'almost done'. Either fix it so it meets the standard, or it is not done.

explain.body: The Definition of Ready is the team's shared agreement on what an item needs before work begins: clear objectives and scope, the information and resources needed, and dependencies in place.

test.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team agrees that no story for the new engineer parts list can be started until Coastline has confirmed the format of list it will accept. Which agreement is the team applying?
test.why: The Definition of Ready covers what must be in place, including dependencies, before work on an item begins (9.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: The Definition of Done decides when an item is complete, not when it can start.
whyNot.1: The quality management approach sets out quality methods and responsibilities, not this team's start criteria.
whyNot.2: The commercial management approach covers supplier contracting; the team's start rule is part of its DoR.

explain.body: The quality register logs quality activities: method, dates, who, result and records. The product register lists each product a plan requires and its status, including approval and acceptance dates.

test.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's head of store operations wants to check the results of the stock accuracy audits carried out in the 10 pilot stores, including which audits failed. Which artifact should hold this information?
test.why: The quality register records each quality activity with its method, dates, responsibilities and pass or fail result (Table 9.1).

whyNot.0: The product register shows each product's status, not the results of individual audits.
whyNot.2: The product backlog holds prioritized user stories, not records of quality checks.
whyNot.3: The project canvas sets out the business justification, not quality results.

explain.body: Time and cost are fixed. Scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves, so when time runs short, lower-priority items give way first.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team forecasts that it cannot finish every story planned for Release 1 by the fixed date. The stories have been prioritized with MoSCoW. Which stories should give way first?
test.why: Scope is flexed for Should and Could haves while Must haves are fixed; Could haves are the first to give way (Table 3.1, 9.3.2).

whyNot.1: Must haves are the fixed part of scope; dropping them would breach the minimum the release must deliver.
whyNot.2: Size does not decide what is dropped; priority does.
whyNot.3: When a story was added says nothing about its priority.

explain.body: Technical debt accumulates interest, making later changes harder. A tolerance can be set for it; if the debt is forecast to become too significant, it causes an exception and the project manager reports it to the board.

test.q: Larkspur Rail's app team now forecasts that its technical debt will exceed the tolerance the board set, so the remaining Must have stories for Release 2 cannot be delivered by the fixed date. Which report should the project manager produce?
test.why: When technical debt is forecast to exceed its tolerance it causes an exception, and the exception report informs the board with options and a recommendation (9.4.2, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: Highlight reporting (the project dashboard) gives regular status; a forecast breach of tolerance needs an exception report.
whyNot.1: An issue report analyses a single issue's impact and options; a forecast tolerance breach at plan level is an exception.
whyNot.3: A lessons report shares lessons for future ways of working; it does not escalate a tolerance breach.
